title: Clarifying Questions Check
description: Predict which clarifying questions actually reduce ambiguity before coding.

questions.prompt: Why do interviewers often leave coding prompts underspecified on purpose?

options.text: To see whether the candidate asks questions that surface real ambiguities before coding
Because writing a fully specified prompt is too much work
Underspecified prompts are always a mistake and should be reported
So candidates are forced to guess without asking anything

questions.explanation: Ambiguity is often intentional — it tests whether the candidate identifies and resolves unknowns (constraints, edge cases) before diving into code.

questions.prompt: "So I need to find the top K most frequent words, right?" — what's the main problem with this as a clarifying question?

options.text: It's too short
It restates the prompt without reducing any real ambiguity
It should not use the word "words"
Nothing — this is a strong clarifying question

questions.explanation: Restating the prompt doesn't narrow any unknown (size, ties, case sensitivity) — a strong question targets a specific constraint or example.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the strongest clarifying question for "top K most frequent words"?

options.text: "Is this a hard problem?"
"If two words tie in frequency, does the order between them matter?"
"Do I need to use JavaScript?"
"Can you repeat the question?"

questions.explanation: This targets a concrete ambiguity (tie-breaking behavior) that changes the correct implementation — a real constraint, not a restatement.

questions.prompt: Why is confirming a concrete example ("for `["a","b","a"]` with K=1, the answer is `["a"]`, correct?") often the highest-value question?

options.text: It wastes time the interviewer would rather spend elsewhere
It exposes mismatched assumptions on both sides before any code is written
Examples are never useful in interviews
It replaces the need for any other clarifying question

questions.explanation: A concrete example forces both sides to agree on input/output shape and edge-case behavior immediately, catching misunderstandings early.

questions.prompt: What should you do if you decide not to ask about every possible ambiguity before starting?

options.text: Say nothing and hope the interviewer doesn't notice
State your working assumption out loud (e.g., "I'll assume case-insensitive unless told otherwise")
Always ask every possible question, no matter how many
Refuse to start coding until every ambiguity is resolved

questions.explanation: Narrating an assumption is a form of communication that keeps momentum while still surfacing your reasoning to the interviewer.

questions.prompt: Which pair of question types does the lesson identify as most likely to reduce real ambiguity?

options.text: Questions about constraints and questions that propose a concrete example
Questions about the interviewer's mood and the room temperature
Questions that simply repeat the prompt word for word
Questions about unrelated topics to build rapport

questions.explanation: Constraint questions (size, case, ties, format) and example-confirmation questions both target concrete unknowns rather than restating the prompt.
